checkpoints: Two operations — decide and record — wrap the model call, sharing exactly one store as the single source of truth.

decide(userId, estimatedInputTokens) runs strictly before any work is sent to the provider, checking the user's rate-limit state (a token bucket, allowing burst while bounding sustained rate) and their accumulated spend.
decide returns {allowed:true, remaining} if both checks pass, or {allowed:false, code, ...} if either fails, with code distinguishing RATE_LIMITED (retryAfterSec) from BUDGET_EXCEEDED (spent/limit).
Refusing to start is the point: if the budget is already exhausted, the call never reaches the model at all — checking afterward means the money is already gone.
record(userId, actualUsage, costMicroUsd) runs strictly after the call completes, pricing from the usage the provider actually reports rather than the estimate that only gated admission.

record appends to the exact same running total the next decide call reads, tracked as an integer (micro-USD, not a float) so there is no window where a request is counted but not blocked, or the reverse, and the number can never quietly drift from what was actually recorded.
Both bucket state and spend are keyed by user identity, since isolating one user's overuse from everyone else is the entire reason the guard exists.
The store can scale from an in-memory map to a shared store (e.g. Redis) with an atomic refill-and-consume operation without changing decide/record's shape.
The design driver is that at any moment the client must know the stream's true state.
A token event carries {token, index}, where index is monotonically increasing — making order verifiable, gaps detectable, and later usable as a resume cursor.
A done event carries {tokenCount} as an explicit success signal, letting the client verify it received every token rather than guess.
An error event carries {code, message} as a unified, machine-readable envelope, so a mid-stream break is never mistaken for a normal ending.
A stream has exactly three terminal outcomes — done, error, or client abort — and once aborted, no further frame (including done) is sent.
On cancellation, the server must observe the client disconnecting and propagate that as an abort into the provider call so generation (and billing) actually stops, with all writes ceasing instantly.

Infrastructure clauses belong in the contract itself: heartbeats (periodic comment frames) defeat intermediary timeouts while the model 'thinks', no-cache/no-transform defeats proxy buffering or re-chunking, and reconnect resumes from the last event id (the index) rather than replaying from scratch.
The channel is deliberately one-way over plain HTTP — the only 'message' the client ever sends upstream is closing the connection.
Treat the prompt as untrusted input, full stop.
The injection scan runs first and matches two separate rules: instruction-override ("Ignore all previous instructions") and system-prompt-leak ("reveal the system prompt").
The pipeline blocks fail-closed right there: no PII redaction runs, and the provider is never called.
The caller gets back status: blocked with a warning naming both attack classes.
The email never goes anywhere — not because it was redacted, but because the flow stopped dead at step 1, before redaction had a chance to run.

On a clean version of this same prompt (no injection phrases, just the email), the email would have been replaced with a [EMAIL] placeholder before the prompt crossed the trust boundary, because past that point it can be logged, retained, or routed through hops you don't control.
The audit log records the block along with the matched substrings that tripped it, never the raw PII, never the raw attack text beyond what's needed to prove why it was blocked.

The ordering (injection first, PII second) is the whole point: reverse it and you waste redaction work on prompts you're about to throw away, and a slipped-through attack would carry the victim's PII out with it.
The provider's quota is account-wide — it cannot single out which user of yours is abusing it, and it only blocks after you have already paid up to that ceiling.
A per-request timeout doesn't help either, since it only bounds the duration of one call, not the number of requests or the total cost.
To actually stop this you need your own admission-control layer placed BEFORE the model call, with three checkpoints in cheap-first, expensive-last order.

The first checkpoint is a token bucket keyed by userId (burst up to capacity, refill = sustained rate, one token spent per request, empty bucket returns 429 with Retry-After); running before any model-calling logic, it rejects the script-looping abuser at near-zero cost while per-user keying leaves everyone else unaffected.

The second checkpoint treats budget as an admission gate, not an after-the-fact report: read the user's running spend against the limit BEFORE reaching the model and refuse with 429/BUDGET_EXCEEDED at the cap, and the total it reads must be exactly what the cost log (priced per token, per tier) accumulates — one source of truth.

The third checkpoint is a timeout with fallback on the model call itself: put a deadline on the primary model, abort it on overrun with no further billing for a discarded result, then degrade to a cheaper fallback model so the request still gets served.

The unifying principle: each checkpoint sits as early as it can because earlier is cheaper when it fires — rate limiting blocks before CPU is spent, the budget gate blocks before money is spent, and timeout-with-fallback handles the one thing that can't be blocked earlier while keeping the request alive; "the provider already has a quota" cannot substitute since it knows nothing about your individual users or requests.

The drop-the-threshold proposal treats the wrong disease: top-k retrieval always returns the k nearest chunks whether or not the question is in the documents at all — a completely off-topic question still has its own "nearest", just with a very low relevance score.

Removing the threshold means every question gets answered, even when nothing is truly relevant, so it worsens exactly the second symptom (confident answers off the wrong document) instead of fixing it.

The real knob is the threshold, and it trades off two opposite errors: too high discards genuinely relevant chunks (lost recall, wrongful "not found"); too low lets loosely-related chunks through and lets the model answer wrong (lost faithfulness).
Product's two complaints don't contradict — they're the two ends of the same axis, which tells you the current threshold is simply mis-set, not that the system is wrong in principle.

Top-k can't replace the threshold because the two knobs measure different things: top-k bounds how many chunks you consider, while the similarity threshold is an absolute floor on relevance, and only it can answer "is the nearest chunk good enough to be worth answering from".
A truthful "I don't know" (grounded=false) is safe and verifiable — the user knows the system had no basis and goes elsewhere.
A confident answer off the wrong document is worse than silence, because it's trusted with no way to detect the error — in sensitive domains like policy or legal, that's the most expensive failure.

The right move is to tune the threshold against real data (measuring over a labeled set of on-topic and off-topic questions to see what each direction of drift costs, stacking a re-rank or hybrid search on top if needed) rather than removing it, since dropping it just swaps one error for a worse one.
Pick the transport by the shape of the data flow: LLM tokens flow one way, server to client, so SSE — a one-way event stream over plain HTTP — is the simplest fit.
SSE traverses proxies as ordinary HTTP, and the browser client auto-reconnects via EventSource, optionally resuming from a Last-Event-ID.

WebSocket buys full-duplex, but at the cost of its own protocol and infrastructure, justified only when the client also continuously pushes data upstream (collaborative editing, two-way realtime chat, shared cursors).
A buffered JSON reply is right when the data is small and complete right now; with an LLM it means a blank screen for the entire generation time, losing the whole point of rendering token by token.
Operationally, a long-lived stream forces you to defeat proxy/CDN buffering, solved with no-cache, no-transform plus flushing after every frame so tokens don't pile up before being pushed.
It also forces you to defeat idle timeouts between tokens while the model is "thinking", solved with periodic heartbeat frames so intermediaries don't assume the connection died and cut it.
That's part of the cost of the SSE choice, not a reason to avoid it.
Both teammates are half right, and neither gets to the real architecture.

Against teammate A: the model cannot be its own gatekeeper, because it is trained precisely to follow instructions in the text it reads, so the line between a legitimate instruction and a trick is blurry from the inside — defense has to live outside the model, at the system layer, before any model call happens.

Against teammate B: yes, a fixed regex is bypassable with odd spelling, another language, or encoding, but that doesn't make the rule layer useless — it is deterministic, essentially free, runs on every request, and fails closed, making it the correct cheap floor, not the whole fence.
On top of that floor, normalize input (lowercase, strip zero-width characters) before scanning so trivial obfuscation doesn't slip through unnoticed.
Layer a model-based classifier on top to catch semantic variants no fixed pattern can enumerate.
The same discipline has to apply to the output side too — PII or a leaked instruction can surface in the model's response, not only in the prompt, so redaction/moderation runs both ways.

The senior-level move is architectural: grant the model the least power it needs, so that even a successful injection cannot execute a dangerous action, because eventually some trick gets past every filter, and damage reduction is what actually holds when detection fails.
That guarantee costs something: accept the occasional false positive, a harmless prompt blocked by mistake, as the price of never letting a matched attack through.

An SSE streaming handler has two independent lifecycles running side by side — the HTTP connection to the client and the token-generation loop pulling from the provider — and nothing links them unless code explicitly bridges the two.

An AbortController that is instantiated and correctly threaded into a provider's streamCompletion(...) call is not sufficient on its own; the controller only stops generation once something actually calls .abort() on it.

A framework does not automatically translate a client-side disconnect (closing the tab, tearing down a fetch) into an abort signal — that translation requires an explicit listener such as req.on("close", () => abortController.abort()).

Without a close-listener wired to the abort controller, abortController.signal.aborted never flips to true, so a for-await loop over the provider stream keeps pulling and writing tokens until the provider naturally finishes, even though the client already left.

Writing SSE frames to a connection nobody is reading and letting generation run to completion after a disconnect means that, with a real provider, the full completion still gets billed even though the response is discarded.

The fix requires two things together: registering an abort trigger on the connection's close event (or an equivalent request-scoped cancellation token/context the platform ties to the connection) and continuing to pass that same abort signal into the provider call exactly as before.

Checking abortController.signal.aborted before each write inside the streaming loop lets the loop break out immediately on cancellation rather than waiting for the next token from the provider, and that same check should guard against sending a terminal "done" frame after an abort.

Correct verification for this kind of fix is starting a stream, aborting after the first token, and confirming the server log stops at a low token count with an aborted/warning line and no "done" event — instead of continuing on to the full token count as if the client never left.

pgvector's `<=>` cosine-distance operator returns a value where a SMALLER number means the two vectors are more alike (0 for identical direction), which is the opposite of what a similarity score means.
Similarity is derived from distance as `1 - distance`, so it points the opposite direction from distance: a LARGER similarity value means more relevant, not less.

In `searchSimilar`, the SELECT projects `embedding <=> $1::vector AS score`, handing `score` the raw distance value, while `.filter((chunk) => chunk.score >= SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD)` is written as if `score` were a similarity — comparing a distance with `>=` against a similarity threshold inverts relevance.

This single inversion produces both symptoms at once: an on-topic chunk with a tiny distance (e.g. ~0.05) fails `0.05 >= 0.3`, gets filtered out, leaves zero chunks, and forces the `grounded=false` fallback even though the right document was retrieved.

An off-topic, near-orthogonal chunk with a large distance (e.g. ~0.6) passes `0.6 >= 0.3`, survives the filter, gets fed into the augmented prompt, and causes the LLM to answer confidently while citing an unrelated document.

`ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector` ranks strictly by ascending distance, so the closest chunk is always first before `LIMIT` cuts the top-k — the ordering logic is correct and is not the source of either bug.

The fix restores the missing distance-to-similarity conversion, e.g. rewriting the projection as `1 - (embedding <=> $1::vector) AS score` inside the same SQL query with no application-layer change needed, while the `ORDER BY` clause and the `>=` comparison stay untouched since only the meaning of `score` needs to change.

Proving the fix closes both bug reports requires an e2e regression pair rather than a single test: a known on-topic query must return `grounded: true` with the expected citation, and a known off-topic query must return `grounded: false` with empty citations, since testing only one direction would not catch the inversion resurfacing.

A guard that protects an expensive call must run as an admission check before that call executes, not as a report computed after the call already happened - a check placed after the provider call has already spent the money it was supposed to prevent spending.

In this handler, `this.cost.priceOf(result)` runs and `this.spentDollars` is updated right after `completion.complete(prompt)` returns, and only afterward is `spentDollars` compared against `budgetLimitDollars` - so the provider call and its cost are always paid before the budget is checked, guaranteeing the cap is overshot by at least one full paid request every time it is crossed.

Because the rejection only fires after the spend already happened, the caller whose request actually pushed spending over the budget still gets served in full; only their next request receives the 429 - enforcement lags one request behind the violation it is meant to prevent.

The fix is to turn the budget check into an admission gate: read the accumulated spend, compare it to the limit, and throw `429 BUDGET_EXCEEDED` (with the spent and limit figures in the response body) before `completion.complete` is ever invoked, the same way the rate-limit check already runs ahead of the handler's real work.

`remainingRequests` is a single field on the service instance with no `userId` anywhere near it, so every caller shares the same counter - one user issuing enough requests can exhaust the allowance meant for the entire user base, leaving everyone else rate-limited by someone else's traffic.

Per-user rate limiting requires keying the counter by `userId` (e.g. a `Map<string, Bucket>` token bucket); once the service runs more than one replica, that state can no longer live on `this` - each instance would keep its own counter and silently multiply the real limit by the replica count, so the bucket state has to move to a shared store like Redis with an atomic refill-and-consume operation.

`spentDollars` accumulates as a floating-point dollar amount on every call (`+= costDollars`), and floating-point addition of many small fractional values drifts away from the true total over time, so the number the budget guard compares against the limit can quietly disagree with what was actually billed.

Money should be accumulated as an integer unit such as micro-USD (`spentMicroUsd += 660`) rather than a float, since integer arithmetic has no rounding drift and keeps the figure the budget guard reads and the figure the cost log reports as one consistent, drift-free source of truth.
